book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: When the same vectors disagree
episodes.subtitle: Cosine, dot product, and the meaning of a score

scenes.title: A collection becomes a constellation
scenes.claim: Encode passages in advance; encode the query when it arrives
scenes.narration: Imagine a library transformed into a constellation. Each passage becomes a stored vector, and a new question becomes another. A bi-encoder makes those representations independently. Now search needs a comparison rule. Different rules can make the very same constellation produce different leaders.

scenes.title: Cosine asks which way you point
scenes.claim: Cosine compares direction and divides out both vector lengths
scenes.narration: In our two-dimensional toy, every vector is an arrow from the same origin. Cosine similarity compares their directions. A smaller angle gives a higher score. Stretching an arrow without changing its direction leaves the cosine unchanged. Length has been divided out.

scenes.title: Three landmarks on the cosine scale
scenes.claim: Same direction: 1 · Perpendicular: 0 · Opposite: −1
scenes.narration: Arrows pointing the same way have cosine one. A right angle gives zero. Turn beyond ninety degrees and the value becomes negative, reaching minus one for opposite directions. These are landmarks of the comparison rule, not percentages of relevance or truth.

scenes.title: Dot product keeps the length
scenes.claim: Multiply matching coordinates, then add the products
scenes.narration: Dot product multiplies each pair of matching coordinates and adds the products. Direction still matters, but length matters too. For our toy query, one comma zero, candidate A scores zero point nine. Candidate B scores one, even though its direction is less closely aligned.

scenes.title: Same candidates, different winner
scenes.claim: Toy calculation: cosine favours A; unnormalised dot product favours B
scenes.narration: Watch the ranking flip. A is better aligned, so cosine ranks A first. B is longer, so the unnormalised dot product ranks B first. No passage changed, and no new relevance judgement arrived. We changed only the numerical comparison rule.

scenes.title: Unit length makes the rules agree
scenes.claim: For unit-length query and candidates: dot product = cosine
scenes.narration: Normalise the query and every candidate to length one. Dot product and cosine now become numerically identical. But a production model may have learnt to use magnitude. Its comparison rule and normalisation should match its training setup; changing them can change the behaviour.

scenes.title: More coordinates, the same arithmetic
scenes.claim: Anonymous toy axes; real embeddings may have hundreds of coordinates
scenes.narration: Add a third coordinate, then hundreds more. The arithmetic still compares matching coordinates and combines the results. Our screen can show only a simplified view. These anonymous axes are not labelled concepts, and the diagram is not a measured projection of a real model.

scenes.title: A score belongs to its own world
scenes.claim: Similarity is a model-and-rule-dependent signal, not a relevance probability
scenes.narration: A similarity score belongs to the representation and rule that produced it. Scores from different models or searches need not be comparable. Nearby can mean a promising candidate, but it cannot certify relevance. Next, our constellation grows too large to search casually.

episodes.title: Searching a hundred million vectors
episodes.subtitle: Exact search, approximate neighbours, and top-k

scenes.title: The encoder is only the beginning
scenes.claim: A search system must store vectors, compare them, and choose leaders
scenes.narration: An encoder is not yet a search system. A collection-scale service must store vectors, compare new queries, and choose where the result list stops. Our warehouse of paper astronauts already has its passage vectors. The question is how to find nearby candidates quickly.

scenes.title: There is no posting list for a meaning
scenes.claim: Lexical route: terms → postings · Dense route: query vector → comparisons
scenes.narration: An inverted index can jump from an analysed term to records containing that term. Dense coordinates provide no equivalent word-to-document pointer. A passage can be close to the query without sharing its words. The engine has to search for nearby vectors instead.

scenes.title: The exact baseline visits everyone
scenes.claim: Toy Euclidean search: examine all six points → return A, B, C
scenes.narration: Exact flat search compares the query with every stored vector. In this toy, smaller Euclidean distance wins. We examine all six points and return A, B, and C. The result is exact under this distance rule, which still does not guarantee usefulness to a reader.

scenes.title: A shortcut can miss a true neighbour
scenes.claim: Illustrative run: examine A, B, D, F → return A, B, D; C is missed
scenes.narration: Now take an illustrative shortcut. We examine A, B, D, and F, but never visit C. Three results still emerge: A, B, and D. C was closer than D. This is a possible approximate-search miss, not a simulation of HNSW or a claim that every run misses.

scenes.title: Navigate a graph instead of scanning
scenes.claim: HNSW uses a navigable graph with multiple layers
scenes.narration: HNSW is one approximate nearest-neighbour approach. It organises vectors into a navigable graph with multiple layers, using connections to explore promising neighbours. Other approaches partition space, compress vectors, or combine strategies. This schematic shows the navigation idea, not the exact path of a real index.

scenes.title: Search effort and output size are separate
scenes.claim: Both toy runs request k = 3; they examine different numbers of points
scenes.narration: Search effort and output size are separate controls. Our exact run examined six points, while the shortcut examined four. Both requested three leaders. An approximate index changes how the engine searches. The requested top k says how many leaders it should return.

scenes.title: Top-k is an output boundary
scenes.claim: Candidate admission · Scoring rule · Search execution · Output size
scenes.narration: Keep four decisions apart. Who is allowed to compete? What rule scores them? How does the engine search? How many leaders are requested? Boolean filters, lexical scores, dense vectors, and hybrid retrieval can all produce top-k outputs. The letter k does not identify an architecture.

scenes.title: Nearest can still be nowhere near useful
scenes.claim: Unless a filter narrows the collection, every stored vector can be scored
scenes.narration: Dense retrieval has no comparable term-match floor. Unless a filter narrows the collection, every stored vector can receive a similarity score. Even an unrelated passage is nearest if everything else is farther away. Nearest means best available under a rule, not necessarily relevant.

episodes.title: Where does meaning enter search?
episodes.subtitle: Semantic goals, compression, and result boundaries

scenes.title: Semantic search names a goal
scenes.claim: Meaning-aware matching can enter at different stages
scenes.narration: A search box accepts a natural-language question. A product promises semantic search. Neither tells you how candidates are retrieved. Semantic describes a goal: matching by meaning. Dense describes a representation. To understand a system, follow the stages where meaning actually enters.

scenes.title: One goal, three possible routes
scenes.claim: Expand and match · Compare dense vectors · Retrieve and rerank
scenes.narration: Take heart attack treatment and a passage using myocardial infarction therapy. Expansion can add vocabulary before lexical retrieval. A trained dense retriever may bridge the phrasing directly. A semantic reranker can compare an already retrieved candidate more carefully. These are possible routes, not guaranteed matches.

scenes.title: Different words can land together
scenes.claim: A suitably trained model may bridge vocabulary without word overlap
scenes.narration: The chapter's question asks whether I am being delulu about getting this job. A useful passage discusses unrealistic expectations during a job search. A suitably trained encoder may bring them together. That vocabulary bridge is valuable, even though similar meaning still does not establish task relevance.

scenes.title: A whole passage, squeezed into one point
scenes.claim: Single-vector encoding compresses the passage before any query arrives
scenes.narration: Precomputation has a price. One pooled vector must stand for a passage's topic, entities, claims, qualifications, and terminology before any query arrives. Broad similarity may dominate an exact identifier, a rare name, or a negation. Shorter chunks reduce this pressure, but each remains a compressed representation.

scenes.title: Why not set one similarity threshold?
scenes.claim: A range search is possible; a useful threshold requires calibration
scenes.narration: A range search can return everything above a chosen similarity threshold. The difficulty is calibration. Scores vary across queries, models, and collections. The same threshold may return nothing for one question and thousands for another. A fixed k gives a more predictable output size.

scenes.title: Every handoff can have its own budget
scenes.claim: Illustrative pipeline: retrieve 30 → select 5 → show 3
scenes.narration: A pipeline can have several boundaries. In this invented example, thirty candidates enter a later stage, five reach an answer writer, and three appear on screen. These are separate budgets. A reranker cannot recover a passage excluded upstream, and the visible count does not reveal how many were examined.

scenes.title: A name and a count do not reveal the machinery
scenes.claim: Chapter snapshots: Semantic Scholar 2025 · OpenAlex Alice 2026
scenes.narration: The chapter contrasts documented snapshots. Semantic Scholar's twenty twenty-five main relevance pipeline begins with lexical candidates, then LightGBM reranking. OpenAlex Alice's twenty twenty-six route begins with embeddings and cosine comparison. The product name, natural wording, and result count alone cannot establish which architecture produced a search.

scenes.title: Ask what competes, what scores, and what stops
scenes.claim: Inspect the pipeline; test relevance against your own task
scenes.narration: Ask what unit each vector represents, which model and comparison rule it uses, whether search is exact or approximate, and where each result boundary sits. Dense retrieval can bridge phrasing, but compress details and miss neighbours. The next chapter opens the stored representation and indexed unit themselves.
